text:
All tests pass.

**Root cause:** In `TTLCache.expire()`, the loop condition used `time > curr.expires` to decide whether an item should be treated as expired, while `__contains__`, `__getitem__`, and `__iter__` all used the stricter `not (time < link.expires)` (i.e., expire when `time >= expires`). This meant that when `time == expires` (e.g. an item set at t=0 with ttl=2, checked at t=2), membership/iteration already considered it expired, but `expire()` did not remove it until `time` strictly exceeded `expires` (t=3). This caused `len()`/`currsize` (which rely on `expire()`) to disagree with `__contains__`/`__iter__`.

**Fix:** Changed the condition in `TTLCache.expire()` from `time > curr.expires` to `not (time < curr.expires)`, matching the expiration semantics used elsewhere in the class so all views agree on when an item expires.

All tests pass.

**Root cause:** In `TTLCache.expire()`, the loop condition used `time > curr.expires` to decide whether an item should be treated as expired, while `__contains__`, `__getitem__`, and `__iter__` all used the stricter `not (time < link.expires)` (i.e., expire when `time >= expires`). This meant that when `time == expires` (e.g. an item set at t=0 with ttl=2, checked at t=2), membership/iteration already considered it expired, but `expire()` did not remove it until `time` strictly exceeded `expires` (t=3). This caused `len()`/`currsize` (which rely on `expire()`) to disagree with `__contains__`/`__iter__`.

**Fix:** Changed the condition in `TTLCache.expire()` from `time > curr.expires` to `not (time < curr.expires)`, matching the expiration semantics used elsewhere in the class so all views agree on when an item expires.
